title: A Path Forward: The Blueprint to Close Rikers
plain_title: A plan to close the Rikers jails and replace them with borough jails
what_they_audited: A report from the Independent Rikers Commission, a panel re-appointed by the City Council speaker, setting out a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex and replace it with borough jails and secure treatment beds, with proposals for the courts, the Department of Correction, city and state health and housing programs and the future of the island. The cover carries only a month, March 2025, so the date here is set to the first of that month.
background: The commission was first established in 2016 by then-Council Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito and was re-appointed in October 2023 by Speaker Adrienne Adams to re-examine the closure plan after COVID-19, spending over a year on research, analysis and consultations. New York City law mandates that the Rikers jails close by August 31, 2027, and the city is building four borough jails plus secure treatment beds at three public hospitals to replace them.

findings.plain: The jail population stands above 6,800, which the commission says is larger than public safety requires and larger than the borough-based system being built can reasonably hold. Major crime in February 2025 was 2.5 percent above February 2020 while the average daily jail population was 25 percent higher.
findings.quote: a jail population that is artificially inflated beyond what is necessary to ensure public safety

findings.plain: Most people in the jails have a mental illness and about 1,400 have a serious mental illness, a share that has grown since the closure plan became law in 2019.

findings.plain: Criminal cases take far longer than they should to resolve, so people wait in jail and crime victims wait for outcomes. More than 1,400 people had been held pretrial for over a year and 500 for over two years.
findings.quote: pretrial has been in jail for 269 days and counting waiting for their day in court.

findings.plain: Every replacement facility is behind schedule, so the 2027 closure deadline will not be met. The Brooklyn jail is slated for 2029, the Bronx for 2031 and Queens and Manhattan for 2032, and the first completed hospital-based treatment units at Bellevue sit unstaffed.
findings.quote: New York City will not meet the 2027 closure deadline

findings.plain: Violence in the jails remains high and discipline is slow on both sides. A federal judge held the city in contempt in the Nunez case, and the court monitor found that of roughly 1,000 full investigations into potential improper uses of force in the first half of 2024, only 16 percent were finished within the mandatory 120 days.
findings.quote: the opportunity for timely discipline has clearly been lost.

findings.plain: The Department of Correction has one of the highest staffing ratios of any jail system in the country, yet sick leave, modified duty and other absences leave about 4,900 uniformed staff available, and attrition far outpaces hiring.
findings.quote: one of the most richly staffed jails in the country.

findings.plain: Rikers costs more than $400,000 per incarcerated person a year, and the commission projects the replacement system would cost far less to run than the debt payments it would add.

recommendations: Close the Rikers Island jail complex as soon as possible.

Move to the borough-based system now under construction, with 4,500 jail and secure hospital treatment beds, and expand the replacement system to 5,000 beds by adding 500 secure psychiatric treatment beds outside the jails.
Cut the number of jail beds planned for women at the Queens facility from 450 to about 250, and redesign or separate the freed space to house men.
Leave the law requiring the Rikers jails to close by August 31, 2027 in place until the City Council and the administration agree on a path forward that assures progress on all fronts.

Speed jail construction by about a year by using the design-build contracts fully, starting foundations and exteriors while interior designs are finalized, following the approach the Port Authority uses.
Apply value engineering, a top-to-bottom review by outside experts of construction, timeline and program plans, to the new jails.
Reorganize Department of Correction staff so the finished treatment units at Bellevue Hospital open within a few months, after correction and health care staff have trained together on the units.
Permanently shutter and decommission space on Rikers as each new borough facility opens, and transfer it to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services.
Shorten the longest criminal cases toward average targets of 90 days for misdemeanors, 180 days for nonviolent felonies, 365 days for violent felonies other than homicide and 730 days for homicides.
Fully staff the New York City Police Department units that hand required evidence to prosecutors, and pass legislation giving prosecutors direct access to police databases.
Finish rolling out the technology that lets police, district attorneys and defense lawyers review and transfer evidence.
Give incarcerated people a secure way to review the evidence in their own cases, such as through the tablets the Department of Correction provides.
Have the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and the police crime lab deliver testing on time, with hiring and retention incentives where needed.

Give the New York State Office of Court Administration additional funds to fully staff, implement, analyze and publicly report on its case processing initiative, including more judges or court personnel if justified.
Speed up court-ordered mental competency exams, known as 730 exams, from an average of 31 business days to 10 business days, and explore changes to the competency process in state law.

Double pretrial electronic monitoring capacity to 800 people citywide over three years, target it at people who would otherwise be jailed, pair it with community-based support and case management and study its effect on rearrests, compliance and court appearance.
Expand the Supervised Release intensive case management pilot to all boroughs, and fund caseworkers to keep working with participants for at least 90 days after their criminal case is resolved.

Increase the capacity of treatment courts for people with serious mental illness and addiction, settle the remaining issues in the state Treatment Court Expansion Act and create more specialized housing and residential treatment for the people those courts serve.

Expand alternative to incarceration and re-entry programs focused on mental illness, addiction and reoffending, clear up contract processing and payment delays for the nonprofits that run them and offer management training to newer, smaller providers.

Expand the work release program under Article 6-A of state correction law for people serving city sentences of less than a year, with individualized release decisions, and use the Local Conditional Release Commission to plan re-entry for sentenced people.

Open 500 secure forensic psychiatric treatment beds outside the jails, ideally at a state facility in or near New York City, primarily for people too severely mentally ill to understand their court cases, phasing in 400 beds over three years on top of the 100 beds proposed for Wards Island, and explore Medicaid reimbursement for that care.
End the waitlists for mobile mental health treatment teams, with the city and state working out how, including paying nonprofit providers enough to recruit and keep staff.

Open 250 residential treatment beds in the community for people with serious mental illness and co-occurring addiction, and if the Hope House pilot in the Bronx succeeds, support similar facilities in each borough plus an option for people awaiting trial who do not want to plead guilty.

Expand and strengthen supportive housing for people with serious mental illness, bring the 380 long-promised Justice Involved Supportive Housing units online as JISH-plus beds with single rooms, flexible services, onsite clinical care and a clubhouse community and build peer staff into the program.
Provide the five hours of daily programming for people in custody that city law sets, and have the City Council set aside a fixed share of the Department of Correction budget for programming.

Provide re-entry planning and services to people leaving Rikers, starting with those serving city sentences, including an early holistic needs assessment, a housing, employment, education and health care plan and certified peer specialists who meet people before release.

Grow the pipeline of health care and correctional workers by recruiting as early as middle and high school, offering benefits to people who stay three to five years and opening new training programs and schools.

Begin changing Department of Correction operations and culture immediately, focusing on accountability through strong management and performance measurement, rethinking key policies and practices, revamping recruitment and hiring and improving education, training and support for staff.

Turn one existing jail on Rikers into a laboratory for reform and a model jail within six months, with policies developed jointly by officers, health care and civilian staff, unions, currently and formerly incarcerated people and their families, service providers and attorneys.

Test in that jail steady posts on steady teams, mentoring for officers and supervisors, incentives for good staff performance, earned privileges for incarcerated people, swift and graduated discipline, 10-hour shifts, wider Crisis Intervention Training, leadership training for captains, regular performance evaluations and more individual choice and responsibility for incarcerated people.
Standardize practice across all the jails by running the department as a high reliability organization, so staff can move between units without learning a different approach to the same issues.
Seek correctional and health care accreditation, such as from the National Commission on Correctional Health Care.

Give officers and other staff mental health support from providers not affiliated with the department, and write standard procedures that connect officers to care immediately after a traumatic incident.

Reward staff for initiative, de-escalation and leadership, let incarcerated people earn and lose privileges and impose swift, certain, graduated discipline on both, moving anyone accused of serious misconduct out of the post or housing area where it happened.

Adopt new Department of Correction and Correctional Health Services policies so that deadlocking, shutting people with serious mental illness in their cells for days or weeks at a time, no longer occurs.
Work with the unions and their members on educational and career support incentives for staff who stay three to five years, and consider condensed workweeks, to slow attrition and attract recruits.
Offer Crisis Intervention Training to many more staff and look outside the department for training models.
Produce up-to-date staffing plans for every facility and specialized unit that account for physical layout, safety and service needs, and base budget requests on those analyses.

Staff the new borough-based system using direct supervision at roughly 0.72 officers for every incarcerated person, about 3,240 uniformed staff for a population of 4,500, with civilian staffing at about today's budgeted level.

Design the new facilities around direct supervision, a town center with clinical, pharmacy and programming space, normalized fixtures, comfortable visitation rooms, outdoor space and daylight and easy maintenance, with the city Department of Correction and the New York State Commission of Correction treating those principles as foundational.

Have New York State apply for a Section 1115 Medicaid waiver so the program covers most treatment and re-entry costs in the last 90 days of a person's incarceration, and bill Medicaid for care of incarcerated people under 21 and many former foster care youth up to age 26.
Reduce Department of Correction overtime toward its average per uniformed staff member in the five years before COVID-19.

Reallocate the $225 million set aside for a correction training academy to other parts of the borough-based system, since the department can keep using the police academy and will need less space for hands-on jail training.
Invest in the four neighborhoods hosting the new jails, especially Chinatown and Mott Haven, including meeting every promise in the 2019 Points of Agreement.

Ease the construction and operating burden on those neighborhoods, for example by leasing nearby garage space for staff vehicles, and keep reporting to residents on construction progress and environmental and noise conditions.

Commit to Renewable Rikers, turning the island after the jails close into a hub for wastewater treatment, composting, solar power and battery storage, and begin master planning, including through legislation that locks in a schedule.
Build the recommendations of the Rikers Island Advisory Committee, created by the 2021 Renewable Rikers Act, into that master planning.

Transfer every part of Rikers no longer in active use from the Department of Correction to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services on the six-month cycle the Renewable Rikers Act sets out, and publish the evaluations of buildings and land behind those decisions.

Set a demolition timeline as part of master planning, with rolling demolition as jails close and early geotechnical and environmental testing to identify landfill risks such as methane and carcinogens.
Use land on Rikers already transferred for interim projects such as solar arrays, battery storage, solar canopies over parking lots and an expanded composting facility.
Recruit and train people from the surrounding neighborhoods, and people who were previously incarcerated or worked on Rikers, for Renewable Rikers construction and permanent jobs.

Set a detailed planning schedule and report regularly to the City Council and the public on the redevelopment, with measurable success indicators, transparent decisions and consistent community engagement.

Appoint a full-time senior official at City Hall whose sole mission is closing Rikers, with funding for dedicated staff, the standing to convene city and state stakeholders, frequent public progress reports and a schedule for the phased closure and demolition of the jails.

Appoint a senior official at the Department of Correction, with a dedicated team, whose sole job is preparing the department for the move to the borough facilities, from training to staffing analysis to operational and cultural change.
Open 500 emergency housing beds with few or no barriers to entry and services on site, at least 250 of them for people with serious mental illness.
Add 500 transitional housing beds with services on site, at least 250 for people with serious mental illness, and provide discharge planning to everyone in transitional housing.
Expand programs that connect people released at arraignment with services, along the lines of the Rapid Response Treatment pilot in Manhattan and the Atlas programs.
Provide family reunification and wraparound support for 500 people recently released from jail, along the lines of the Osborne Association's kinship re-entry program.

Provide at least 1,000 permanent housing vouchers set aside for people leaving Rikers or living in emergency or transitional housing, with Correctional Health Services and the Department of Homeless Services identifying homeless people before release.
Offer landlords and brokers incentives to rent to formerly incarcerated people, including help with minor repairs, paperwork and deposits.

Offer everyone jailed after their Supreme Court arraignment a holistic needs assessment within 14 days covering mental and physical health, substance use, possible intellectual disability and histories of domestic violence and abuse, and use it to inform charging, detention, release and plea decisions.
Provide court and case explainers and system navigators for incarcerated people, crime victims and family members, written for varying literacy levels and disabilities.
Establish borough-based population review teams that bring justice system players together to examine individual cases for safe diversion or resolution, with particular attention to women.

Screen people for open warrants and police I-Cards at Supreme Court arraignment and resolve them while the criminal case is pending, so no one is held after the case ends on a warrant or card no longer being pursued.

Ensure New York State has enough entry-level prison beds for specialized groups, such as people receiving medication assisted treatment, people with serious mental illness and transgender people, so sentenced people do not wait at Rikers for a transfer.
Pass legislation letting people in jail earn merit time credits off their sentences for taking part in educational, vocational and rehabilitative programs.
Increase support for crime victims, who reported losing jobs and housing after a crime, rarely receiving state compensation and seldom getting mental health support or counseling.
Expand residential drug treatment beds in the jails beyond the two units now open, one with 50 beds for men and one with 50 beds for women.
